title: To amend the FISA Amendments Act of 2008 to extend the authorities of title VII of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978 through April 30, 2026, and for other purposes.
official_title: To amend the FISA Amendments Act of 2008 to extend the authorities of title VII of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978 through April 30, 2026, and for other purposes.
summary: Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act lets the Attorney General and the Director of National Intelligence jointly authorize, for up to one year at a time, the targeting of persons reasonably believed to be located outside the United States to acquire foreign intelligence information. They may do that on an order issued under subsection (j)(3), or on their own determination that exigent circumstances exist, and nothing in subchapter I of FISA requires an application for a court order for an acquisition targeted that way. The prohibitions the statute writes are specific rather than general: no intentional targeting of anyone known to be located in the United States, no targeting a person outside the United States in order to reach a particular known person here, no intentionally acquiring communications that contain a reference to, but are not to or from, a target, no intentionally acquiring a communication where the sender and all intended recipients are known to be in the United States, and the acquisition must be conducted consistent with the Fourth Amendment. FBI personnel may query what was collected using a U.S. person query term after prior approval from an FBI supervisor or attorney, unless they have a reasonable belief the query could assist in mitigating or eliminating a threat to life or serious bodily harm. This bill extends that authority through April 30, 2026 with no new limits, oversight requirements, or reforms added.
brief: Extends Section 702 of FISA — the Attorney General and the Director of National Intelligence jointly authorizing the targeting of people reasonably believed to be located outside the United States, with no application for a court order required for such an acquisition — through April 30, 2026, with no reforms attached.

top_lines.headline: What Section 702 Does
subs: The Attorney General and the Director of National Intelligence authorize jointly, for up to one year at a time, the targeting of persons reasonably believed to be located outside the United States to acquire foreign intelligence information — on an order issued under subsection (j)(3), or on their own determination that exigent circumstances exist
Nothing in subchapter I of FISA is to be construed to require an application for a court order for an acquisition targeted at a person reasonably believed to be located outside the United States

The same two officials may direct an electronic communication service provider, in writing, to immediately provide the Government with all information, facilities, or assistance necessary to accomplish the acquisition, in a manner that will protect the secrecy of the acquisition and produce a minimum of interference with the services the provider is providing to the target

The acquisition may not intentionally target anyone known to be located in the United States, may not target a person outside the United States in order to reach a particular known person here, may not intentionally acquire communications that contain a reference to, but are not to or from, a target, may not intentionally acquire a communication where the sender and all intended recipients are known to be in the United States, and must be conducted consistent with the Fourth Amendment

FBI personnel must obtain prior approval from an FBI supervisor or attorney before a query of what was collected using a U.S. person query term, unless they have a reasonable belief the query could assist in mitigating or eliminating a threat to life or serious bodily harm; the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court reviews those querying procedures under subsection (j)

top_lines.headline: What This Bill Changes
subs: Extended through April 30, 2026 — no new limits or reforms
Considered and passed the House April 16, the Senate April 17, approved April 18, 2026

sections.label: Section 1 — Extension of Title VII Authorities

items.main: Section 702 was added to title VII of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act by the FISA Amendments Act of 2008 (Public Law 110-261), the Act this bill amends, so extending title VII extends Section 702. The extension runs through April 30, 2026 with no new conditions attached.
items.detail: Amends Section 403(b) of the FISA Amendments Act of 2008 (Public Law 110-261) in both of its paragraphs. Paragraph (1), the 50 U.S.C. 1881 note, has "effective two years after" and everything following it through the end of the sentence struck, replaced by "effective April 30, 2026, title VII of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978 (50 U.S.C. 1881 et seq.) is repealed." Paragraph (2), the 18 U.S.C. 2511 note, has "Effective two years after the date of enactment of the Reforming Intelligence and Securing America Act--" replaced by "Effective April 30, 2026--". Section 1(b) separately amends Section 404(b), rewriting the transition-procedure heading and replacing its cross-references with a direct citation to (50 U.S.C. 1881 et seq.). The amendments take effect on the earlier of the date of enactment or April 19, 2026. No new minimization requirements, no new oversight mechanisms, and no restrictions on FBI queries of the collected data are included.

underreported: Section 1(b) also rewrites Section 404(b) of the FISA Amendments Act of 2008, the transition procedures: the heading loses its reference to the Reforming Intelligence and Securing America Act, and the cross-references to that Act, to the FISA Amendments Reauthorization Act of 2017 and to section 101(a) become a direct citation to (50 U.S.C. 1881 et seq.). The bill's title mentions only the extension.
gaps: The bill extends Title VII surveillance authorities through April 30, 2026 but sets no reporting requirement on how those authorities are used during the extension period.
The bill sets a fixed April 30, 2026 expiration date but does not establish any conditions or framework governing further reauthorization after that date.
